name: -thing ADJ
title: Compound Pronoun + Adjective (something interesting)
description: Indefinite pronouns ending in -thing (something, nothing, anything, everything) are followed directly by an adjective instead of the adjective coming before, as with normal nouns.
example: Let's do something fun this weekend.

name: ACCUSATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: that
title: Object Relative Pronoun (that)
description: Use 'that' to introduce a relative clause when the noun it refers to is the object of the following verb or preposition; it is often dropped in informal speech.
example: The car that I bought last month broke down.

name: ACCUSATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: which
title: Relative pronoun 'which' (object)
description: 'Which' can introduce a relative clause where it functions as the object of the clause's verb, referring to a thing mentioned earlier.
example: This is the book which I borrowed from you.

name: ACCUSATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: who
title: Relative pronoun 'who' (object)
description: 'Who' can introduce a relative clause where it stands for the object of the clause's verb, common in informal speech in place of 'whom'.
example: She's the friend who I met in Spain.

name: ACCUSATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: whom
title: Relative pronoun 'whom' (object)
description: 'Whom' introduces a relative clause as the object of the verb or preposition inside it; it is formal and used mainly in writing.
example: He's the man whom I saw yesterday.

name: ADJ/ADV enough (except for 'not enough')
title: Adjective/Adverb + enough
description: 'Enough' follows an adjective or adverb to mean 'to the necessary degree', often followed by 'to + verb' to show the result or purpose.
example: She's old enough to drive now.

name: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: as
title: As-clauses (reason and time)
description: Use 'as' to introduce a clause giving a reason ('because') or describing an action happening at the same time ('while').
example: As I was tired, I went to bed early.

name: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: as soon as
title: As soon as (time clauses)
description: 'As soon as' introduces a clause meaning immediately after something happens, using present tense even when referring to the future.
example: Call me as soon as you arrive.

name: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: by the time
title: by the time (+ clause)
description: Introduces a time clause meaning 'no later than when X happens', typically paired with a perfect tense to show one event finished before another.
example: By the time we arrived, the film had started.

name: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: if
title: If-clauses (conditionals)
description: Join an 'if' clause to a main clause to talk about real possibilities or imagined situations and their results.
example: If it rains, we'll stay at home.

name: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: so that
title: So that (purpose clauses)
description: 'So that' introduces a clause of purpose, usually with 'can/could/will/would', explaining the reason behind an action.
example: I saved money so that I could travel this year.

name: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE: when
title: Time Clauses with 'When'
description: A clause beginning with 'when' shows the time something happens and can come before or after the main clause.
example: When I get home, I cook dinner.

name: ADVERBS OF ATTITUDES: apparently/clearly/fortunately/frankly/unfortunately
title: Attitude Adverbs (fortunately, clearly, frankly...)
description: Sentence adverbs like apparently, clearly, fortunately, frankly and unfortunately, usually placed at the start, show the speaker's opinion or attitude toward the whole sentence.
example: Unfortunately, I can't come to the party.

name: ADVERBS OF FREQUENCY: always/usually/often/frequently/occasionally/sometimes/rarely
title: Adverbs of Frequency (always, usually, sometimes...)
description: These adverbs say how often something happens and are usually placed before the main verb but after the verb 'be'.
example: I usually wake up at seven.

name: ADVERBS OF NEGATION: never
title: Adverb 'never'
description: 'Never' means 'at no time' and is placed before the main verb, or after 'be', to make a strong negative statement.
example: I never eat breakfast.

name: ADVERBS OF QUASI-NEGATION: hardly/little/scarcely/seldom
title: Quasi-negative Adverbs: hardly, scarcely, seldom, little
description: These adverbs give a sentence a near-negative meaning without using 'not', showing that something is almost never true or true to a very small degree.
example: I hardly ever go out on weeknights.

name: ADVERBS: INTENSIFIERS: extremely/greatly/really/so/terribly/too/unbelievably/very
title: Intensifiers (very, really, too, so)
description: These adverbs go before an adjective or another adverb to make its meaning stronger or, with 'too', to show excess.
example: This coffee is really hot.

name: AS IF/THOUGH+SECOND CONDITIONAL
title: As if / As though + Past Simple
description: Uses 'as if' or 'as though' with a past-tense verb to describe an unreal or unlikely comparison, even when the situation is present.
example: He talks as if he knew everything.

name: ASK/TELL+NP+to+INFINITIVE
title: Ask/Tell + Someone + To-Infinitive
description: Use 'ask' or 'tell' followed by a person and a to-infinitive to report a request or instruction given to that person.
example: I asked him to close the door.

name: AUX+PERFECT
title: Modal + have + past participle (modal perfect)
description: A modal verb followed by 'have' and a past participle, used to make guesses, criticisms, or talk about unfulfilled possibilities in the past.
example: He must have forgotten about our meeting.

name: AUX+PROGRESSIVE
title: Modal + be + -ing (modal progressive)
description: A modal verb followed by 'be' and an -ing form, used to guess or comment on an action that may be happening right now or later.
example: She might be sleeping right now.

name: Am I ...?
title: To Be: Am I ...? (yes/no question)
description: Invert 'am' and 'I' to form a yes/no question about yourself in the present.
example: Am I late?

name: Am I not ...?
title: To Be: Am I not ...? (formal negative question)
description: A negative question asking for confirmation about yourself; formed by adding 'not' after 'am I'.
example: Am I not right?
note: Rare, formal wording; conversational learners should use the natural equivalent 'Aren't I...?' instead.

name: Are these/those ...?
title: Questions with 'Are these/those...?'
description: Put 'are' before 'these' or 'those' to ask a yes/no question about plural objects or people.
example: Are these your books?

name: Are they ...?
title: Yes/No Questions: 'Are they...?'
description: Put 'are' before 'they' at the start of a sentence to ask a yes/no question with the verb 'to be'.
example: Are they your classmates?

name: Are we ...?
title: To Be: Are we ...? (yes/no question)
description: Invert 'are' and 'we' to ask a yes/no question about a group that includes the speaker.
example: Are we late?

name: Are you ...?
title: To Be: Are you ...? (yes/no question)
description: Invert 'are' and 'you' to ask a yes/no question about the listener in the present.
example: Are you ready?

name: Aren't these/those ...?
title: Negative Questions: 'Aren't these/those...?'
description: Use the contracted negative 'aren't' before 'these/those' to ask a negative question about plural things, often to confirm.
example: Aren't those your gloves?

name: Aren't they ...?
title: Negative Questions: 'Aren't they...?'
description: Use the contracted negative 'aren't' before 'they' to ask a negative yes/no question, often to check or confirm something.
example: Aren't they coming to the party?

name: Aren't we ...?
title: To Be: Aren't we ...? (negative question)
description: The contracted negative question form used to check or confirm something about a group that includes the speaker.
example: Aren't we friends?

name: Aren't you ...?
title: To Be: Aren't you ...? (negative question)
description: The contracted negative question form used to check an assumption or express mild surprise about the listener.
example: Aren't you hungry?

name: BE about to DO
title: Be about to (near future)
description: Formed with 'be' + about to + base verb; used to say that something is going to happen very soon.
example: Hurry up, the movie is about to start.

name: BE to DO
title: Be + To-Infinitive (formal plans)
description: Uses 'be' followed by a to-infinitive to describe official arrangements, plans or instructions, mostly in formal or written English.
example: The president is to visit Paris next week.

name: COMPARATIVE OF SUPERIORITY: -er
title: Comparative Adjectives (-er)
description: Add '-er' to short adjectives to compare two things or people, often followed by 'than'.
example: This bag is bigger than that one.

name: COMPARATIVE OF SUPERIORITY: more+ADJ/ADV
title: Comparative with more (more + adjective/adverb)
description: Longer adjectives and adverbs form the comparative with 'more' instead of adding '-er', used to compare two things.
example: This lesson is more interesting than the last one.

name: COMPARATIVE and COMPARATIVE (the same adjective)
title: Repeated Comparatives (bigger and bigger)
description: Repeating the same comparative adjective or adverb joined by 'and' shows a quality that keeps increasing or decreasing over time.
example: The traffic is getting worse and worse.

name: COMPARATIVE/SUPERLATIVE OF INFERIORITY
title: Comparative and Superlative of Inferiority: less/least
description: Formed with 'less + adjective/adverb + than' or 'the least + adjective/adverb', this shows that something has a smaller degree of a quality than another.
example: This option is less expensive than the other one.

name: COMPARISON OF EQUALITY: as ... as
title: Comparison of Equality: as ... as
description: Formed with 'as + adjective/adverb + as', this pattern says two things are equal in some quality; 'not as ... as' shows they are unequal.
example: This restaurant is as good as the one downtown.

name: COMPARISON OF EQUALITY: not as/so ... as
title: Comparison of Equality: not as/so ... as
description: 'Not as/so + adjective/adverb + as' compares two things that are unequal, saying the first has a lower degree of the quality than the second.
example: This flat isn't as big as our old one.

name: COMPOUND RELATIVE PRONOUN:
title: What as a Relative Pronoun (the thing that)
description: 'What' can mean 'the thing(s) that', introducing a clause that works as the subject or object of the sentence.
example: I don't know what you mean.

name: CONDITIONAL: SECOND
title: Second Conditional (If + past, would + verb)
description: Used for unreal or unlikely present/future situations: 'if' + past simple in the condition clause, 'would' + base verb in the result clause.
example: If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.

name: CONDITIONAL: THIRD
title: Third Conditional (If + past perfect, would have + past participle)
description: Used to imagine a different past and its unreal result: 'if' + past perfect in the condition clause, 'would have' + past participle in the result clause.
example: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.

name: COORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS
title: Coordinating Conjunctions (and, but, or, so)
description: Words like 'and', 'but', 'or' and 'so' join two words, phrases or independent clauses of equal grammatical status.
example: I like tea, but I don't like coffee.

name: DEFINITE ARTICLES
title: Definite Article (the)
description: 'The' is used before a noun that is specific or already known to the listener, whether singular, plural, or uncountable.
example: The book on the table is mine.

name: DETERMINER: another
title: Determiner: another
description: 'Another' means 'one more' or 'a different one'; it goes before a singular countable noun or stands alone as a pronoun.
example: Can I have another cup of tea, please?

name: DETERMINER: no
title: Determiner 'no' (no money, no time)
description: 'No' goes before a noun to mean 'not any', letting you make a sentence negative without using 'not' or 'don't'.
example: I have no time today.

name: DETERMINERS: some/any
title: Some / Any
description: 'Some' is used in affirmative sentences and offers, while 'any' is used in negative sentences and questions, with countable or uncountable nouns.
example: I don't have any milk, but I have some juice.

name: Do+IMPERATIVE
title: Emphatic Imperative (Do + verb)
description: Adds 'do' before an imperative verb to add emphasis, insistence or politeness in spoken requests and invitations.
example: Do sit down and make yourself comfortable.

name: ELLIPTICAL ACCUSATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN
title: Omitting the Relative Pronoun (Contact Clauses)
description: When the relative pronoun is the object of its own clause, it can be dropped, as in 'the book I read' instead of 'the book that I read'.
example: Where's the pen I gave you?

name: EXCLAMATION: How ADJ/ADV ...!
title: Exclamations with How + Adjective/Adverb
description: Start an exclamation with 'How' followed directly by an adjective or adverb to express a strong reaction like surprise or admiration.
example: How amazing this view is!

name: EXCLAMATION: What ...!
title: Exclamations with 'What...!'
description: Use 'What' plus a noun phrase (sometimes followed by subject and verb) at the start of a sentence to express surprise or strong feeling, ending in an exclamation mark.
example: What a beautiful day!

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Can I ...?
title: Functional Question: Can I...? (asking permission)
description: 'Can I' plus the base verb is a common spoken formula for asking permission or making a simple request.
example: Can I open the window, please?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Can you ...?
title: Requests with 'Can you...?'
description: 'Can you...?' is a common, friendly way to ask someone to do something for you.
example: Can you help me with this bag?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Can't you ...?
title: Requests with 'Can't you...?'
description: A negative question form used to make a request sound more persuasive or to show mild frustration about something not being done.
example: Can't you help me carry these bags?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Could I ...?
title: Functional Question: Could I...? (polite permission)
description: 'Could I' plus the base verb is a more polite way to ask permission or make a request than 'Can I'.
example: Could I have some water, please?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Could you ...?
title: Polite Requests with 'Could you...?'
description: 'Could you' plus the base verb is a common, polite way to ask someone to do something for you.
example: Could you pass me the salt, please?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Couldn't you ...?
title: Requests with 'Couldn't you...?'
description: A negative question with 'could' used to make a softer but slightly pressing request or suggestion.
example: Couldn't you just call him instead of emailing?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: May I ...?
title: Asking Permission with 'May I...?'
description: 'May I' plus the base verb is a polite, somewhat formal way to ask for permission to do something.
example: May I open the window, please?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Shall I ...?
title: Shall I ...? (offering to do something)
description: Uses 'Shall I' plus the base verb to offer to do something for the listener, inviting them to agree or decline. Common in everyday offers of help.
example: Shall I carry that bag for you?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Shall we ...?
title: Shall we ...? (making a suggestion)
description: Uses 'Shall we' plus the base verb to suggest an activity for both speaker and listener to do together. Common in casual invitations and plans.
example: Shall we go for a walk later?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Should I ...?
title: Should I ...? (asking for advice)
description: Uses 'Should I' plus the base verb to ask the listener for their opinion or advice about an action. Very common when unsure what to do.
example: Should I call him now or wait?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Why don't we ...?
title: Why don't we ...? (suggesting a joint activity)
description: Uses 'Why don't we' plus the base verb to propose an activity for speaker and listener together, softer than a direct suggestion.
example: Why don't we order pizza tonight?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Why don't you ...?
title: Why don't you ...? (giving suggestions/advice)
description: Uses 'Why don't you' plus the base verb to suggest an action to the listener in a friendly, informal way, similar to giving advice.
example: Why don't you take a break for a while?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Will you ...?
title: Requests with 'Will you...?'
description: 'Will you...?' is used to make a request or to ask about someone's willingness to do something.
example: Will you close the door, please?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Won't you ...?
title: Invitations with 'Won't you...?'
description: A negative question with 'will' used to make a friendly invitation or offer, expecting the listener to agree.
example: Won't you join us for dinner tonight?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Would you ...?
title: Would you ...? (polite requests/invitations)
description: Uses 'Would you' plus the base verb to politely ask someone to do something or invite them to do something. Common in offers, requests and invitations.
example: Would you like some more tea?

name: FUNCTIONAL QUESTION: Wouldn't you ...?
title: Persuasive Questions with 'Wouldn't you...?'
description: A negative question with 'would' used to persuade someone or to check that they agree with an idea.
example: Wouldn't you like a cup of coffee?

name: GENITIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN
title: Relative Pronoun 'whose'
description: 'Whose' introduces a relative clause showing possession, replacing a possessive adjective, and is followed directly by a noun.
example: That's the neighbor whose dog barks all night.

name: GET+NP+PRESENT PARTICIPLE
title: get + object + -ing
description: 'Get' followed by a noun or pronoun and an -ing verb means to cause someone or something to start doing an action.
example: He got the whole class laughing.

name: GET+PAST PARTICIPLE
title: Get-Passive (get + past participle)
description: Uses 'get' instead of 'be' before a past participle, common in informal spoken English for things that happen, often suddenly or unexpectedly.
example: He got hurt playing football yesterday.

name: HAVE/GET+NP+PAST PARTICIPLE
title: Causative (have/get something done)
description: Use 'have' or 'get' plus a noun plus a past participle to say someone else performs an action for the subject, rather than doing it themselves.
example: I need to get my phone screen repaired.

name: HAVE/LET/MAKE+NP+INFINITIVE
title: Causative Verbs (have/let/make someone do)
description: Have, let and make are followed by a person and a base-form verb to show that someone causes, allows or forces another person to do something.
example: My boss made me stay late.

name: I am
title: To Be: I am (present simple)
description: Use 'am' with the subject 'I' to state identity, feelings, or states in the present. It is the only present-tense form of 'to be' used with 'I'.
example: I am a teacher.

name: I am not
title: To Be: I am not (negative)
description: Add 'not' after 'am' to make a negative statement about yourself; in speech it is almost always shortened to 'I'm not'.
example: I'm not tired.

name: IF ONLY+SECOND CONDITIONAL
title: If only + past simple (present wish)
description: 'If only' plus a past-tense verb expresses a strong wish that a present situation were different, more emphatic than 'I wish'.
example: If only I had more free time!

name: IF ONLY+THIRD CONDITIONAL
title: If only + past perfect (past regret)
description: 'If only' plus the past perfect expresses strong regret about something that did or did not happen in the past.
example: If only I had studied harder back then.

name: IF+SHOULD (e.g. if it should rain tomorrow)
title: If + should (unlikely future condition)
description: Adding 'should' after 'if' in a future conditional makes the condition sound less certain, often used in formal suggestions or instructions.
example: If you should see her, say hello for me.

name: IMPERATIVE: AFFIRMATIVE (lexical verbs)
title: Imperative (Commands)
description: Use the base form of the verb to give commands or instructions, and add 'don't' before the verb for negative commands.
example: Come in, but don't sit there.

name: INDEFINITE ARTICLES
title: Indefinite Articles (a/an)
description: 'A' and 'an' go before a singular countable noun to mean one non-specific thing; 'an' is used before a vowel sound.
example: I have a dog and an apple.

name: INDEFINITE PRONOUN/PROP-WORDS: ones (except for 'one')
title: Substitute pronoun: ones
description: 'Ones' replaces a plural countable noun already mentioned, often after 'the', 'these/those', 'which' or an adjective.
example: I don't like these shoes, I prefer the black ones.

name: INDEFINITE PRONOUN: none
title: Indefinite Pronoun: none
description: 'None' means 'not any' or 'not one' and stands in for a noun already mentioned, used with a singular or plural verb depending on meaning.
example: I asked for help, but none of my friends answered.

name: INDEFINITE PRONOUNS
title: Indefinite Pronouns (somebody, anything, nobody...)
description: Formed by combining some-/any-/no-/every- with -thing, -one, or -body; used to talk about unspecified people or things.
example: Somebody left their bag here.

name: INDIRECT QUESTION: ASK/REMIND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL
title: Indirect Questions after Ask/Remind/Show/Teach/Tell
description: Report a question as the object of verbs like ask, remind, show, teach, or tell, introduced by if, whether, or a question word, using statement word order.
example: She asked me if I was ready.

name: INDIRECT QUESTION: DECIDE/EXPLAIN/KNOW/LEARN/SEE/UNDERSTAND/WONDER
title: Indirect Questions (I wonder where...)
description: After verbs like decide, explain, know, learn, see, understand and wonder, a question is embedded with normal word order, introduced by if, whether or a question word.
example: I wonder where he lives.

name: INDIRECT SPEECH: SAY/EXPLAIN/REPORT
title: Reported Speech (say, explain, report)
description: Report what someone said using verbs like say, explain or report followed by a that-clause, often shifting the tense back from the original words.
example: She said that she was tired.

name: INDIRECT SPEECH: TELL
title: Reported Speech with Tell
description: Use 'tell + person + (that) + clause' to report what someone said, usually shifting the verb tense back one step from the original words.
example: She told me that she was tired.

name: INTENSIFIED COMPARATIVES: a lot/by far/even/far/much/still
title: Intensified Comparatives (much, far, even, a lot)
description: Words like much, far, even, still, a lot and by far go before a comparative adjective or adverb to strengthen the degree of difference between two things.
example: This restaurant is much better than the last one.

name: INTENSIFIED SUPERLATIVES: by far/far/far and away/much
title: Intensified Superlatives: by far, much, far and away
description: Words like 'by far', 'much', and 'far and away' strengthen a superlative, emphasizing that something is clearly the greatest or best.
example: She is by far the best singer in the group.

name: INVERSION: CONDITIONAL WITH SHOULD (e.g. Should it rain tomorrow.....)
title: Inversion: Should + subject (formal conditional)
description: Dropping 'if' and inverting subject and 'should' creates a formal conditional meaning 'if it should happen', typical of written or formal English.
example: Should you need help, just call me.

name: INVERSION: Hardly/Little/Never/No sooner/Scarcely/Seldom ....
title: Negative adverbial inversion (Never have I...)
description: Placing a negative adverb like 'never', 'hardly' or 'no sooner' at the start of a sentence for emphasis triggers inversion of subject and auxiliary verb.
example: Never have I seen such a mess.

name: INVERSION: neither/nor+BE/HAVE/DO/AUX+PERSONAL PRON
title: Neither/Nor + Auxiliary + Subject (agreeing with negatives)
description: After a negative statement, 'neither' or 'nor' plus an auxiliary verb plus the subject shows the same negative is true for someone else.
example: I don't like coffee. Neither do I.

name: INVERSION: so+BE/HAVE/DO/AUX+PERSONAL PRON
title: So + Auxiliary + Subject (agreeing with positives)
description: After a positive statement, 'so' plus an auxiliary verb plus the subject shows the same is true for someone else, with the subject and verb inverted.
example: I love this song. So do I.

name: Is he/she ...?
title: To Be: Is he/she ...? (yes/no question)
description: Invert 'is' and the subject to ask a yes/no question about a third person in the present.
example: Is she at work?

name: Is it ...?
title: Yes/No Questions with 'be' (Is it...?)
description: Formed by putting the verb 'be' before the subject; used to ask a yes/no question about something's identity, state, or the weather.
example: Is it your book?

name: Is this/that ...?
title: Questions with 'Is this/that...?'
description: Put 'is' before 'this' or 'that' to ask a yes/no question about a single object or person.
example: Is this your umbrella?

name: Isn't he/she ...?
title: To Be: Isn't he/she ...? (negative question)
description: The contracted negative question form used to confirm an assumption about a third person.
example: Isn't he your brother?

name: Isn't it ...?
title: Negative Questions with 'be' (Isn't it...?)
description: Formed with the contraction 'isn't' before the subject; used to ask a negative yes/no question, often to check or comment on something.
example: Isn't it cold today?

name: Isn't this/that ...?
title: Negative Questions: 'Isn't this/that...?'
description: Use the contracted negative 'isn't' before 'this/that' to ask a negative question, often to confirm what you already think is true.
example: Isn't that your teacher?

name: It is
title: Present Simple: 'It is'
description: Use 'is' with the pronoun 'it' to describe or identify a thing, or to talk about time, weather, or a situation.
example: It is cold today.

name: It is not
title: Basic negation: It is not (impersonal it)
description: The pronoun 'it' plus 'is not' makes a negative statement about a fact, situation, or time, typically at the start of a clause.
example: It is not far from here.
note: Trivial basic negation known well below B2; the sentence-position restriction is a corpus-extraction artifact, not a real grammar point.

name: MODAL/AUX: (have) got to
title: Have Got To (obligation)
description: 'Have got to + base verb' is an informal spoken way of saying 'have to', often contracted to 've got to' or 's got to'.
example: I've got to finish this report today.

name: MODAL/AUX: be able to
title: Be able to (ability)
description: Expresses ability or possibility across different tenses, used where 'can' is not grammatically possible, such as future or perfect forms.
example: I hope I'll be able to help you tomorrow.

name: MODAL/AUX: be going to
title: Be Going To (future plans)
description: Use 'am/is/are + going to + base verb' to talk about future plans, intentions, or predictions based on present evidence.
example: We're going to visit my parents this weekend.

name: MODAL/AUX: can
title: Can (Ability and Permission)
description: The modal 'can' plus a base verb expresses ability, permission or possibility; negate with 'can't' and invert 'can' before the subject to ask questions.
example: Can you help me, please?

name: MODAL/AUX: could
title: Could (past ability, polite requests, possibility)
description: Used as the past form of 'can' for general ability, and also to make polite requests or express possibility.
example: Could you pass me the salt, please?

name: MODAL/AUX: dare (to)
title: Dare (to) as a modal verb
description: 'Dare' can behave like a modal (no -s, no 'to') or like an ordinary verb (with 'to'), meaning to have the courage to do something; most common in negatives and questions.
example: I daren't tell him what really happened.

name: MODAL/AUX: have got to
title: Have Got To: negatives and questions
description: Negative and question forms of the informal obligation modal 'have got to', made with 'not' or by inverting 'have'.
example: Have you got to leave so soon?

name: MODAL/AUX: have to
title: Have To (obligation)
description: Use 'have to + base verb' to express obligation or necessity that comes from outside the speaker, such as rules or circumstances.
example: I have to work early tomorrow.

name: MODAL/AUX: may
title: May (permission and possibility)
description: Used to ask for or give formal permission, and to express that something is possible.
example: You may leave the table when you finish.

name: MODAL/AUX: may as well
title: 'May as well' for lack of a better option
description: 'May as well' + base verb suggests doing something because there is no better alternative or nothing will be lost by doing it; used in statements, negatives and questions.
example: We may as well order dinner while we wait.

name: MODAL/AUX: may well
title: may well (strong probability)
description: 'May well' plus a base verb expresses that something is quite likely to be true or happen, stronger than plain 'may'.
example: She may well be right about the traffic.

name: MODAL/AUX: might
title: Might (possibility)
description: Expresses a weaker, more tentative possibility than 'may', often used to speculate about present or future events.
example: It might snow this weekend.

name: MODAL/AUX: might as well
title: 'Might as well' for lack of a better option
description: 'Might as well' + base verb is a common spoken variant of 'may as well', suggesting an action is worth doing since there is nothing better to do or to lose.
example: You might as well tell me the truth now.

name: MODAL/AUX: must
title: Must (obligation and strong deduction)
description: Expresses strong obligation or necessity, and also strong logical certainty that something is true.
example: You must show your passport at customs.

name: MODAL/AUX: need (to)
title: Need (to) — necessity
description: Use 'need to + base verb' to say something is necessary; in British English 'need' can also work like a modal, e.g. 'needn't'.
example: Do you need to call him tonight?

name: MODAL/AUX: ought to
title: Ought to (advice and obligation)
description: A slightly formal alternative to 'should', used to give advice or express a mild obligation.
example: You ought to apologize to her.

name: MODAL/AUX: shall
title: Shall (suggestions and offers)
description: Use 'shall I/we + base verb' mainly in questions to make suggestions or offers; plain statements with 'shall' are formal and rare today.
example: Shall we get some coffee?

name: MODAL/AUX: should
title: Should (advice and recommendation)
description: Use 'should + base verb' to give advice, make recommendations, or say what is the right or expected thing to do.
example: You should see a doctor about that cough.

name: MODAL/AUX: used to
title: Used to (past habits)
description: Describes past habits, states or repeated actions that no longer happen or are no longer true.
example: I used to play tennis every weekend.

name: MODAL/AUX: will
title: Will (future predictions and decisions)
description: Use 'will + base verb' for predictions, promises, offers, and decisions made at the moment of speaking.
example: I think it will rain later.

name: MODAL/AUX: would
title: Would (polite requests and preferences)
description: Use 'would + base verb' for polite requests and offers ('would you like'), past habits, and the result of hypothetical conditionals.
example: Would you like some tea?

name: NOMINATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN:
title: Relative Clauses with 'That'
description: 'That' introduces a clause describing a person or thing and acts as the subject of that clause, as in 'the book that is on the table'.
example: This is the bus that goes downtown.

name: NOMINATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: which
title: Relative pronoun 'which' (subject)
description: 'Which' introduces a relative clause and acts as the subject of that clause, referring back to a thing or animal mentioned earlier.
example: I bought a car which runs on electricity.

name: NOMINATIVE RELATIVE PRONOUN: who
title: Relative Clauses with 'Who'
description: 'Who' introduces a clause describing a person and acts as the subject of that clause, as in 'the man who lives next door'.
example: I have a friend who speaks French.

name: PARTICIPIAL CONSTRUCTION: PAST PARTICIPLE
title: Past Participle Clauses (Written by...)
description: A past participle placed at the start of a clause replaces 'which was/is' to describe the subject more concisely, often in a slightly formal style.
example: Built in 1990, the house has a beautiful garden.

name: PARTICIPIAL CONSTRUCTION: PRESENT PARTICIPLE
title: Present Participle Clauses (Feeling tired, ...)
description: Begin a sentence with an -ing clause that gives background action or a reason before the main clause, with both parts sharing the same subject.
example: Feeling exhausted, I went straight to bed.

name: PASSIVE: AUX
title: Modal Passive (can/must/should be done)
description: Formed with a modal verb + be + past participle, used to talk about ability, obligation, permission or possibility from the passive viewpoint.
example: The tickets can be bought online.

name: PASSIVE: AUX+PERFECT
title: Modal Perfect Passive (must/should have been done)
description: Formed with a modal verb + have been + past participle; used to speculate, judge or comment on a past action affecting the subject.
example: The email should have been sent yesterday.

name: PASSIVE: DIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS
title: Passive with Thing as Subject (A gift was given to me)
description: The thing being transferred becomes the subject of the passive sentence, with the receiver added after 'to' or 'for', as an alternative to the person-first pattern.
example: A gift was given to every guest.

name: PASSIVE: FUTURE
title: Future Passive with will (will be done)
description: Formed with will + be + past participle; used to say that something will happen to the subject in the future, without naming who will do it.
example: The results will be announced tomorrow.

name: PASSIVE: FUTURE PERFECT
title: Future Perfect Passive (will have been done)
description: Formed with 'will have been' plus a past participle, this says an action will be completed, from a passive viewpoint, before a stated future time.
example: The report will have been finished by Friday.

name: PASSIVE: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE
title: Future Progressive Passive (will be being done)
description: Formed with 'will be being' plus a past participle, this describes an action that will be ongoing and receiving the action at a specific future moment.
example: This time tomorrow, the room will be being cleaned.
note: Extremely rare, clumsy structure even natives avoid; not worth a speaking lesson.

name: PASSIVE: INDIRECT OBJECTS OF GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL AS SUBJECTS
title: Passive with Person as Subject (I was given...)
description: The person who receives something becomes the subject of a passive sentence, common with verbs like give, send, show, teach and tell.
example: I was given a warm welcome at the office.

name: PASSIVE: PAST
title: Past Simple Passive (was/were + past participle)
description: Formed with was/were + past participle, used when the focus is on the action or the receiver of the action rather than who did it.
example: The window was broken during the storm.

name: PASSIVE: PAST PERFECT
title: Past Perfect Passive (had been done)
description: Formed with had + been + past participle; shows that something happened to the subject before another past action or point in time.
example: The tickets had already been sold when we arrived.

name: PASSIVE: PAST PROGRESSIVE
title: Past Progressive Passive (was being done)
description: Formed with was/were + being + past participle; describes an action in progress at a past moment, focusing on the thing affected rather than the doer.
example: The car was being repaired when I called.

name: PASSIVE: PRESENT
title: Present Simple Passive (is/are + past participle)
description: Form the present passive with am/is/are plus a past participle to focus on the action or the receiver rather than who does it.
example: This coffee is made in Brazil.

name: PASSIVE: PRESENT PERFECT
title: Present Perfect Passive (has been done)
description: Formed with has/have + been + past participle; used to talk about a completed action affecting the subject, without naming who did it, with relevance to now.
example: The report has already been finished.

name: PASSIVE: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE
title: Present Progressive Passive (is being done)
description: Formed with am/is/are + being + past participle; used to describe an action happening right now, focusing on the thing affected rather than who is doing it.
example: The kitchen is being renovated this week.

name: PHRASAL VERBS (V+NP+PARTICLE)
title: Phrasal Verbs (verb + object + particle)
description: A verb combines with a particle like 'up', 'off' or 'out' to make a new meaning; the object noun can often go before or after the particle.
example: Can you turn the music down, please?

name: PHRASAL VERBS (V+PARTICLE)
title: Phrasal Verbs (verb + particle)
description: A verb combined with a particle such as up, down, on, or off creates a new meaning, as in 'sit down' or 'turn on'.
example: Please sit down and turn on the light.

name: PHRASAL VERBS (V+PARTICLE+PREP+NP)
title: Three-Part Phrasal Verbs (verb + particle + preposition)
description: A verb is combined with a particle and then a preposition plus an object, as in 'get on with' or 'run out of'.
example: We ran out of milk this morning.

name: POSSESSIVE PRONOUNS (except for 'his' and 'its')
title: Possessive Pronouns (mine, yours, hers, ours, theirs)
description: Possessive pronouns stand alone for a possessive determiner + noun to show ownership without repeating the noun, e.g. 'That's my bag' becomes 'That's mine.'
example: This coat isn't mine, I think it's yours.

name: POSTMODIFYING PAST PARTICIPLE
title: Reduced Relative Clauses with Past Participle
description: A noun can be followed directly by a past participle phrase instead of a full passive relative clause, as in 'the cake made by Tom' for 'that was made by Tom'.
example: The letter written by Tom arrived today.
note: Too advanced for A1 (usually B1/B2); corpus tag is frequently confused with passive and perfect forms.

name: POSTMODIFYING PRESENT
title: Reduced Relative Clauses with -ing
description: A noun can be followed directly by an '-ing' phrase instead of a full relative clause, as in 'the man sitting there' for 'who is sitting there'.
example: I saw a boy playing football.
note: Too advanced for A1 (usually B1); the corpus tag is frequently confused with progressive questions and participle clauses.

name: PREMODIFYING PAST PARTICIPLE
title: Past Participle as Adjective (a broken cup)
description: A past participle can go directly before a noun to describe it, functioning like an adjective, as in 'a broken cup' or 'boiled eggs'.
example: She has a broken phone.

name: PREMODIFYING PRESENT PARTICIPLE
title: -ing Adjectives Before Nouns
description: A present participle (-ing form) can stand directly before a noun to describe it, acting like an adjective.
example: Careful, that's boiling water!

name: PREP+RELATIVE PRONOUN
title: Preposition + Relative Pronoun (to whom/in which)
description: In formal English, a preposition can go directly before the relative pronoun, as in 'to whom' or 'in which', instead of at the end of the clause.
example: She's the colleague with whom I share an office.

name: PREP+V-ING
title: Preposition + -ING (interested in doing)
description: After a preposition, use the -ing form of the verb rather than the to-infinitive, e.g. 'good at', 'before', 'without'.
example: She's good at speaking English.

name: PREPOSITION STRANDING
title: Ending Questions with a Preposition
description: In everyday English, a preposition linked to a question word often stays at the end of the sentence instead of moving to the front.
example: What are you looking for?

name: PREPOSITIONS
title: Basic Prepositions (in, on, at, with, from...)
description: Prepositions show relationships of place, time, direction, or manner between a noun or pronoun and the rest of the sentence.
example: I live in London and work near the station.

name: PRONOUN: others (excluding 'the
title: Pronoun: others (some... others...)
description: 'Others' without 'the' means 'other people or things' in general, often used to contrast with 'some'.
example: Some people love coffee; others prefer tea.

name: PRONOUNS: the other/others
title: the other / the others (pronoun use)
description: Use 'the other' (singular) or 'the others' (plural) alone, without a following noun, to mean the remaining item(s) in a specific set already mentioned.
example: One shoe is here; where's the other?

name: Please+INFINITIVE
title: Please + imperative verb
description: 'Please' is added before or after the base form of a verb in an imperative sentence to make a request sound polite.
example: Please close the door.
note: Politeness marker on the basic imperative (A1 level); not a distinct grammar structure to teach separately at A2.

name: Please+don't/never+INFINITIVE
title: Polite Negative Imperative (Please don't...)
description: Add 'please' before a negative imperative (don't/never + base verb) to soften a request, warning, or instruction.
example: Please don't be late for the meeting.

name: RECIPROCAL PRONOUN: each other
title: Reciprocal Pronoun: each other
description: 'Each other' is used after a verb or preposition to show that two or more people do the same thing to one another.
example: We've known each other since school.

name: RECIPROCAL PRONOUN: one another
title: Reciprocal Pronoun: one another
description: 'One another' shows that two or more people do the same thing to each other; it functions like 'each other', often in slightly more formal contexts.
example: The team members support one another during difficult projects.

name: REFLEXIVE PRONOUNS
title: Reflexive Pronouns (myself, yourself, etc.)
description: Reflexive pronouns ending in -self/-selves show that the subject and object of a verb are the same person, or add emphasis to the subject.
example: I taught myself how to cook.

name: RELATIVE ADVERB: NONRESTRICTIVE
title: Non-Restrictive Relative Clauses with Where/When
description: After a noun phrase, add ', where' or ', when' to give extra, non-essential detail about a place or time already mentioned.
example: We visited Rome, where we ate amazing pizza.

name: RELATIVE ADVERB: WITH
title: Relative Clause with 'when'
description: The relative adverb 'when' follows a time noun (like 'day' or 'year') to add information about it, working much like a conjunction introducing a time clause.
example: I remember the day when we first met.

name: RELATIVE ADVERB: WITHOUT ANTECEDENT
title: Free Relative Clauses with Where/When/Why
description: Use 'where', 'when', or 'why' after 'be' or a preposition to introduce a clause that itself acts as the missing place, time, or reason, without a noun before it.
example: This is where I grew up.

name: RELATIVE PRONOUN: NONRESTRICTIVE
title: Non-Restrictive Relative Clauses (, who/which,)
description: Add extra, non-essential information about a noun using a relative clause set off by commas; the sentence still makes sense if the clause is removed.
example: My sister, who lives in London, is visiting us.

name: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+BECOME/FEEL/GO/LOOK/SEEM/SOUND+COMPLEMENT (ADJ)
title: Linking Verbs + Adjective (look, feel, seem...)
description: Verbs like become, feel, go, look, seem and sound connect the subject to a describing adjective instead of taking a direct object.
example: You look tired today.

name: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+DIRECT OBJECT+to+INDIRECT OBJECT
title: Verb + Direct Object + to + Person (give/send/show...)
description: Use verbs like give, pass, send, show, teach, or tell in the pattern verb + thing + 'to' + person, as an alternative word order to the double-object pattern.
example: He gave the keys to the manager.

name: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+GIVE/PASS/SEND/SHOW/TEACH/TELL+INDIRECT OBJECT+DIRECT OBJECT
title: Verbs with Two Objects (give someone something)
description: Verbs like give, pass, send, show, teach and tell can take an indirect object (the receiver) followed by a direct object (the thing given or sent).
example: Can you show me the photo?

name: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+MAKE+OBJECT+COMPLEME NT (ADJ)
title: 'Make' + Object + Adjective
description: The verb 'make' can be followed by an object and an adjective to show that something causes a change in that object's state or feeling.
example: That song makes me happy.

name: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+V
title: Basic Subject + Verb Sentences
description: A sentence made only of a subject and a simple-tense verb, with no object or complement, e.g. 'Birds fly.'
example: The baby is sleeping.
note: Basic S+V pattern is elementary sentence structure, not a distinct lesson point at B1.

name: SENTENCE PATTERN: SUBJECT+V+OBJECT
title: Basic Word Order (Subject + Verb + Object)
description: English statements follow a fixed Subject-Verb-Object order, with the subject first, the verb second and the object last.
example: She reads a book every day.
note: Basic SVO order underlies every A1 sentence from the very first lesson; not a distinct standalone grammar point.

name: SUBORDINATE CLAUSE: after/albeit/although/because/before/despite/except/for/lest/like/once/since/so/than/though/till/unless/until/where/whereas/wheresoever/whether/while/whilst tagged as IN
title: Subordinating Conjunctions (because, before, after, although...)
description: Words such as 'because', 'before', 'after', 'although' and 'since' introduce a clause that adds a reason, time or contrast to the main clause.
example: I stayed home because it rained.

name: SUPERLATIVE OF SUPERIORITY: -est
title: Superlative Adjectives (-est)
description: Add '-est' to short adjectives, usually with 'the', to show that one thing has the most of a quality among several.
example: This is the tallest building in the city.

name: SUPERLATIVE OF SUPERIORITY: most+ADJ/ADV
title: Superlative with most (most + adjective/adverb)
description: Longer adjectives and adverbs form the superlative with 'the most' instead of adding '-est', used to compare three or more things.
example: That was the most difficult exam I've taken.

name: TAG QUESTION: FOLLOWING AFFIRMATIVE SENTENCE
title: Tag Questions after Affirmative Statements
description: Add a short negative question (auxiliary + n't + subject pronoun) after a positive statement to check information or invite agreement.
example: You like coffee, don't you?

name: TAG QUESTION: FOLLOWING NEGATIVE SENTENCE
title: Tag Questions after Negative Statements
description: Add a short positive question (auxiliary + subject pronoun) after a negative statement to check information or invite agreement.
example: You don't like coffee, do you?

name: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE
title: Future with will and going to
description: Formed with 'will + base verb' for predictions and quick decisions, or 'am/is/are going to + base verb' for plans, plus the future progressive (will be + -ing) for actions in progress in the future.
example: I'm going to visit my parents next weekend.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT
title: Future Perfect (will have done)
description: Formed with 'will have + past participle', it describes an action that will already be completed before a specific point in the future.
example: By next year, I will have finished my degree.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PERFECT PROGRESSIVE
title: Future Perfect Progressive (will have been doing)
description: Formed with 'will have been + verb-ing', it emphasizes the duration of an action that will continue up to a specific point in the future.
example: By June, I will have been working here for five years.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: FUTURE PROGRESSIVE
title: Future Progressive (will be doing)
description: Formed with 'will be' + -ing form, the future progressive describes an action that will be in progress at a specific future time, often used here in questions.
example: Will you be using the car tomorrow morning?

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST (BE)
title: Past Simple: BE (was/were)
description: Use was/were to describe past states, and combine with -ing for past continuous actions in progress; negate with wasn't/weren't.
example: They were at home, and I was watching TV.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT
title: Past Perfect (had done)
description: Formed with 'had' + past participle, the past perfect describes an action completed before another past action or time; 'had been doing' is the progressive form for ongoing past actions.
example: By the time we arrived, the film had already started.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PERFECT PROGRESSIVE
title: Past Perfect Progressive (had been doing)
description: Formed with 'had been + verb-ing', it describes an action that was ongoing up to a point before another past event, emphasizing duration.
example: She had been waiting for an hour when the bus finally arrived.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PAST PROGRESSIVE
title: Past Progressive (was/were doing)
description: Formed with was/were + verb-ing, used to describe an action in progress at a specific moment in the past, often interrupted by another event.
example: I was watching TV when she called.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (BE)
title: Present Simple: BE (am/is/are)
description: Use am/is/are to state facts, identities, or descriptions in the present; add 'not' for negatives and invert subject and verb for questions.
example: She is a teacher, and she isn't busy today.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs)
title: Present Simple & Past Simple (lexical verbs)
description: Use the base verb for habits/facts with I/you/we/they, and the -ed or irregular past form for completed actions; make negatives and questions with do/does/did.
example: I don't work on Sundays, but I worked yesterday.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexical verbs; third person & singular)
title: Present Simple: Third Person Singular (-s)
description: Add -s/-es to the verb for he/she/it in the present simple; form negatives and questions with doesn't/does.
example: She doesn't drink coffee, but she likes tea.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT (lexicalverbs)
title: Present Simple Questions (do-support)
description: A 'Do you...?' question pattern with a lexical verb, duplicating the present simple do-support pattern already taught elsewhere.
example: Do you like coffee?
note: Corpus duplicate/typo of the present-simple lexical-verb item; same pattern already covered there.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT
title: Present Perfect (have/has done)
description: Formed with have/has + past participle, used for past actions connected to now, recent events, or life experiences; includes the present perfect continuous (have been + -ing).
example: I've already finished my homework.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PERFECT PROGRESSIVE
title: Present Perfect Progressive (have/has been doing)
description: Formed with 'have/has been + verb-ing', it describes an action that started in the past and continues, or has just stopped, with effects visible now.
example: I've been studying English for three years.

name: TENSE/ASPECT: PRESENT PROGRESSIVE
title: Present Continuous (be + -ing)
description: Use am/is/are plus verb-ing to talk about actions happening now or temporary situations; negate and question with be.
example: I'm cooking dinner right now.

name: TO-INFINITIVE: WITH NOTIONAL SUBJECT
title: For + Noun/Pronoun + To-Infinitive
description: Adds 'for + noun or pronoun' before a to-infinitive to show who performs the action, often after adjectives like 'important' or 'easy'.
example: It's easy for him to learn languages.

name: TO-INFINITIVE: not to DO
title: Negative To-Infinitive (not to do)
description: Places 'not' before a to-infinitive to negate it, used after verbs like 'decide', 'tell' or 'promise' to express a negative intention or instruction.
example: I promised not to be late again.

name: TO-INFINITIVE: to DO (not preceded by 'not')
title: To-Infinitive of Purpose
description: Use 'to' plus the base verb to explain the purpose or reason for an action, often answering 'why'.
example: I called you to ask about the party.

name: TO-INFINITIVE: to be DONE
title: Passive To-Infinitive (to be done)
description: Formed with 'to be' + past participle after nouns, adjectives or verbs, showing that something still needs to happen to the subject.
example: There's still a lot of work to be done.

name: TO-INFINITIVE: to have DONE
title: Perfect Infinitive (to have done)
description: 'To have' plus a past participle refers to something completed before the main verb's time, often expressing assumption, hope or regret.
example: He seems to have forgotten our meeting.

name: These/Those N
title: Demonstratives: these/those + noun
description: The plural demonstrative determiners 'these' and 'those' go before a plural noun to point to things near or far from the speaker.
example: Those shoes look really comfortable.
note: Elementary demonstrative + plural noun pattern already known by B1; corpus label reflects position/POS extraction limits, not a lesson.

name: These/Those are
title: Demonstratives: 'These/Those are'
description: Use 'these' for nearby plural things and 'those' for plural things farther away, followed by 'are' to describe them.
example: These are my keys.

name: These/Those are not
title: Demonstrative Negatives: 'These/Those are not'
description: Add 'not' after 'are' (or use 'aren't') with 'these/those' to say plural things are not something.
example: Those are not my shoes.

name: This/That N
title: Demonstratives: this/that + Noun
description: Using 'this' or 'that' directly before a singular noun to point to something near or far in space or time.
example: This coffee is too hot for me.
note: Basic demonstrative + noun pattern normally taught at A1; the sentence-position restriction is a corpus extraction artefact, not a teaching point.

name: This/That is
title: Demonstratives: 'This/That is'
description: Use 'this' for something near and 'that' for something farther away, followed by 'is' to identify or describe a single thing.
example: This is my phone.

name: This/That is not
title: Demonstrative Negatives: 'This/That is not'
description: Add 'not' after 'is' (or use 'isn't') with 'this/that' to say a single nearby or distant thing is not something.
example: That is not my bag.

name: V+that+CLAUSE
title: Verb + that-clause (I think that...)
description: Verbs like think, know, hope, say, and believe can take a 'that' clause as their object; 'that' is often dropped in speech.
example: I hope you can come to the party.

name: V-ING (not preceded by 'not')
title: -ING Form (Gerund/Participle)
description: The -ing form of a verb can act like a noun, as in 'Swimming is fun', or describe something, as in 'the sleeping baby'.
example: Swimming is my favorite hobby.

name: V-ING: WITH NOTIONAL SUBJECT (expressed as possessive pronouns)
title: Possessive + Gerund (his/her doing)
description: A possessive pronoun is placed before an -ing form to show whose action is meant, mainly in more formal spoken or written English.
example: I don't mind his coming late for once.

name: VERB OBJECT V-ING
title: Verb + Object + -ing
description: Verbs like 'see', 'watch', 'hear' and 'find' can be followed by an object plus an -ing form to show that the action was in progress.
example: I saw him waiting outside the station.

name: VERB OBJECT not V-ING
title: Verb + Object + not + -ing
description: A verb followed by an object and then 'not' plus a gerund, describing the object not doing something; this corpus pattern mostly captures mis-parsed matches rather than real, frequent usage.
example: I remember him not answering the phone.
note: Mostly mis-parsed corpus matches, not a reliable teaching pattern

name: VERB OBJECT to DO
title: Verb + Object + To-Infinitive (want someone to do)
description: Verbs like want, ask, tell, and need can take an object followed by 'to' plus the base verb, meaning the object performs the action.
example: I want you to help me.

name: VERB V-ING
title: Verb + -ING (enjoy doing)
description: Some verbs, such as enjoy, like, stop, and finish, are followed directly by the -ing form of another verb.
example: I enjoy reading books in the evening.

name: VERB not V-ING
title: Verb + not + -ing (negative gerund)
description: Certain verbs (excluding be/have) can be followed by 'not' plus a gerund to show that an action is avoided or does not happen.
example: I suggested not telling her the bad news yet.

name: VERB not to DO
title: Verb + Not + To-Infinitive
description: Put 'not' before the to-infinitive to make the second verb negative, e.g. after decide, want, or try.
example: I decided not to go to the party.

name: VERB to DO
title: Verb + To-Infinitive (want to do)
description: Some verbs, such as want, like, need, and plan, are followed by 'to' plus the base verb to express intentions or desires.
example: I want to learn English.

name: WH- QUESTION: How ...?
title: Wh- Questions: How...?
description: Formed with 'How' followed by an auxiliary/modal verb, then the subject and main verb; used to ask about manner or method.
example: How do you make this soup?

name: WH- QUESTION: How ADJ/ADV ...?
title: Wh- Questions: How + Adjective/Adverb (How old...?)
description: 'How' is combined with an adjective or adverb (old, much, often, far) to ask about degree, quantity or frequency.
example: How often do you exercise?

name: WH- QUESTION: What ...?
title: Wh- Questions: What...?
description: Formed with 'What' followed by an auxiliary/modal verb, then the subject and main verb; used to ask about things, actions or ideas.
example: What do you want for dinner?

name: WH- QUESTION: What N ...?
title: Wh- + Noun Questions (What time...?)
description: 'What' is placed directly before a noun (time, color, kind, size, etc.) to ask for a specific piece of information.
example: What time does the shop close?

name: WH- QUESTION: When ...?
title: Wh- Questions: When...?
description: Formed with 'When' followed by an auxiliary/modal verb, then the subject and main verb; used to ask about time.
example: When does your class start?

name: WH- QUESTION: Where ...?
title: Wh- Questions: Where...?
description: Formed with 'Where' followed by an auxiliary/modal verb, then the subject and main verb; used to ask about location or place.
example: Where do you live now?

name: WH- QUESTION: Which ...?
title: Questions with 'Which...?'
description: 'Which' asks someone to choose from a known or limited set of options, standing alone as a pronoun at the start of a question.
example: Which do you like better?

name: WH- QUESTION: Which N ...?
title: 'Which + Noun' Questions
description: 'Which' can go directly before a noun to ask someone to pick a specific item from a known set.
example: Which bus goes downtown?

name: WH- QUESTION: Who ...?
title: Wh- Question with Who
description: 'Who' asks about the identity of a person, typically placed at the start of the question and often functioning as its subject.
example: Who left this message for me?
note: Basic question form mastered well before B2; included only as a corpus sentence-position artefact.

name: WH- QUESTION: Whom ...?
title: Questions with 'Whom...?'
description: 'Whom' is the formal object form of 'who', placed at the start of a question when asking about the person affected by the action.
example: Whom did you meet yesterday?

name: WH- QUESTION: Whose ...?
title: Questions with 'Whose...?'
description: 'Whose' asks about ownership and can stand alone as a pronoun at the start of a question.
example: Whose is this jacket?

name: WH- QUESTION: Whose N ...?
title: 'Whose + Noun' Questions
description: 'Whose' can go directly before a noun to ask who owns that thing.
example: Whose bag is this?

name: WH- QUESTION: Why ...?
title: Wh- Questions: Why...?
description: Formed with 'Why' followed by an auxiliary/modal verb, then the subject and main verb; used to ask for a reason or explanation.
example: Why are you so tired today?

name: WH-+to+INFINITIVE
title: WH-word + To-Infinitive (what to do, how to say)
description: Combine a question word like what, how, where, or when directly with a to-infinitive to express what someone should or can do, often after verbs like know, decide, or tell.
example: I don't know what to say.

name: WH-EVER
title: Wh-ever Words (whoever, whatever, whichever)
description: Adding '-ever' to a wh-word gives the meaning 'no matter who/what/which' or 'any one that', used in statements and free relative clauses.
example: You can choose whatever topping you like.

name: WISH+SECOND CONDITIONAL
title: Wish + Past Simple (present wish)
description: 'Wish' followed by a past simple verb expresses a desire for a present situation to be different from reality.
example: I wish I knew how to swim.

name: WISH+THIRD CONDITIONAL
title: Wish + Past Perfect (past regret)
description: 'Wish' followed by a past perfect verb expresses regret about something that did or didn't happen in the past.
example: I wish I had studied harder for that exam.

name: You are
title: Present Simple 'be': You are
description: The subject pronoun 'you' combined with 'are', the present simple form of the verb 'to be', used to make statements about the listener or people in general.
example: You are right about that.
note: Basic present-simple 'be' mastered before B1; label reflects a sentence-initial corpus extraction constraint, not a new teaching point.

name: You are not
title: To Be: You are not (negative)
description: Add 'not' after 'are' to make a negative statement about 'you', usually contracted to 'you're not' or 'you aren't' in speech.
example: You're not late.

name: being+PAST PARTICIPLE
title: Passive Participle Clause (being done)
description: Formed with 'being' + past participle to give a passive reason or background circumstance for the main action, mostly in more formal English.
example: Being asked to leave, he felt embarrassed.

name: did DO
title: Emphatic 'did' (I did do it)
description: Stressed 'did' is placed before the base verb to emphasize that something really happened, often to contradict doubt or a previous statement.
example: I did lock the door, I promise.

name: do/does DO
title: Emphatic do/does (do-support for emphasis)
description: Adding stressed 'do/does' before the base verb in an affirmative sentence emphasizes or confirms the truth of a statement, often contrasting with doubt.
example: I do enjoy spending time with you.

name: few PLURAL NOUN
title: Quantifier: few + plural noun
description: 'Few' (without 'a') means 'not many' or 'almost none' and goes before a plural countable noun.
example: Few people came to the meeting.

name: had it not been for ...
title: 'Had it not been for' (formal inversion)
description: This is the formal, inverted version of 'if it hadn't been for': 'if' is dropped and 'had' moves before the subject to express a past hypothetical dependence on something.
example: Had it not been for her quick thinking, we'd have lost everything.

name: having been+PAST PARTICIPLE
title: Perfect passive participle clauses (Having been + past participle)
description: A reduced clause formed with 'having been' plus a past participle shows an action was completed before the main clause, often giving a reason; the past participle can also function as an adjective.
example: Having been warned about the storm, we cancelled the trip.

name: having+PAST PARTICIPLE
title: Perfect Participle Clause (having done)
description: Formed with 'having' + past participle at the start of a sentence to show that one action finished before another one happened.
example: Having finished dinner, we went for a walk.

name: he/she is
title: To Be: He/She is (present simple)
description: Use 'is' with third-person singular subjects (he, she, it) to state facts, identity, or feelings in the present.
example: She is my sister.

name: he/she is not
title: To Be: He/She is not (negative)
description: Add 'not' after 'is' to make a negative statement about a third person, often shortened to 'isn't' or 'he's/she's not'.
example: He isn't at home.

name: here is/are
title: Here is/are
description: Introduces or points out something nearby using 'here' followed by 'is' or 'are' plus a noun.
example: Here is your coffee, sir.
note: Basic presentational structure normally learned below B1; not a substantive new point at this level.

name: hope/know/think+CLAUSE (without 'that')
title: Omitting 'That' after Think/Know/Hope
description: After verbs like 'think', 'know' and 'hope', the connector 'that' is often left out before the clause that follows in everyday speech.
example: I think it's a good idea.

name: if it hadn't been for ...
title: 'If it hadn't been for' (past unreal condition)
description: This fixed phrase expresses a past hypothetical meaning 'without X having happened', showing that a past result depended on X; it uses the past perfect.
example: If it hadn't been for the delay, we'd have missed the flight anyway.

name: if it were not for ...
title: 'If it were not for' (present unreal condition)
description: This fixed phrase introduces a present hypothetical condition meaning 'without X', showing that something else depends on X's existence; it uses the subjunctive 'were'.
example: If it weren't for your help, I would still be lost.

name: in order to DO
title: Purpose Clause with 'in order to'
description: Placed before a base-form verb to state the reason or purpose for an action; a slightly more formal alternative to 'to' alone.
example: I left early in order to catch the train.

name: it+BE(+ADV)+ADJ(+for+NP)+to+INFINITIVE
title: It + be + Adjective + (for someone) + To-Infinitive
description: Use 'it' as a dummy subject with 'be' and an adjective, optionally adding 'for + person', before a to-infinitive to comment on an action or situation.
example: It's important for you to be on time.

name: it+BE(+ADV)+ADJ+that+CLAUSE
title: It is + adjective + that... (extraposition)
description: 'It' introduces a delayed subject clause after 'be' and an adjective, giving an opinion or reaction about the fact stated in the 'that' clause.
example: It's strange that he hasn't called yet.

name: know/wonder+WH-(CLAUSE) (except for 'whether')
title: Embedded WH-Clauses after Know/Wonder
description: After 'know' or 'wonder', add a wh-word (what, where, why, who, etc.) followed by normal statement word order, not question word order, to talk about information you have or are curious about.
example: I wonder what time the movie starts.

name: let's (not followed by 'not')
title: Let's + Verb (Suggestions)
description: Use 'let's' plus a base verb to suggest doing something together, as in 'let's go'; the negative 'let's not' is a separate pattern.
example: Let's have some coffee.

name: let's not
title: Let's not (negative suggestion)
description: Formed with 'let's not' plus the base verb, used to suggest that a group avoid doing something together.
example: Let's not argue about this again.

name: little UNCOUNTABLE NOUN
title: Quantifier: little + uncountable noun
description: 'Little' (without 'a') means 'not much' or 'almost none' and goes before an uncountable noun.
example: We have little money left this month.

name: me/us/him/her/them (except for 'you' and 'it')
title: Object Pronouns (me, us, him, her, them)
description: Object pronouns replace a noun after a verb or preposition to show who or what receives the action.
example: Can you help me and them tomorrow?

name: much UNCOUNTABLE NOUN
title: Quantifier: much + uncountable noun
description: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns, mainly in questions and negative sentences, to talk about a large quantity.
example: I don't have much time today.

name: my/our/your/her/their (except for 'his' and 'its')
title: Possessive Adjectives (my, our, your, her, their)
description: Possessive adjectives go before a noun to show who it belongs to; they stay the same for singular and plural nouns.
example: This is our house and that is their car.

name: not+V-ING
title: Negative -ing Form (not doing)
description: 'Not' is placed directly before an -ing form to negate a gerund or participle, often introducing a reason or circumstance.
example: Not knowing the address, I got lost.

name: so ADJ/ADV (that) CLAUSE
title: so + Adjective/Adverb (that) + Clause
description: 'So + adjective/adverb (+ that)' introduces a clause that shows the result of a high degree of a quality, e.g. 'so tired that I fell asleep'.
example: She was so tired that she fell asleep on the sofa.

name: so as to DO
title: Purpose clauses with 'so as to'
description: Use 'so as to' + base verb to express purpose, meaning 'in order to'; it is often used with 'not' for negative purpose and sounds a little more formal than 'to' alone.
example: She left early so as to avoid the traffic.

name: such (a/an) ADJ NOUN
title: such (a/an) + Adjective + Noun
description: 'Such' before '(a/an) + adjective + noun' emphasizes the degree of a quality, similar to 'so', often used in exclamations and vivid descriptions.
example: It was such a boring movie that I fell asleep.

name: the COMPARATIVE (...), the COMPARATIVE
title: The Comparative..., the Comparative... (the more, the better)
description: This pattern pairs two comparative phrases to show that a change in one thing causes a related change in another.
example: The more you practice, the better you get.

name: the fact(s) that+CLAUSE
title: The fact that + clause
description: 'The fact that' introduces a noun clause presenting something as true, often used as the subject or object of a sentence in slightly formal speech.
example: The fact that she apologized surprised everyone.

name: there+AUX+be
title: There + Modal + Be
description: Combines 'there is/are' with a modal verb such as 'must', 'might' or 'should' to express certainty, possibility or necessity about existence.
example: There must be another way to solve this.

name: there+be
title: There is / There are
description: 'There' plus a form of 'be' introduces the existence of something; negate with 'isn't/aren't' and invert for questions such as 'Is there...?'.
example: There are two cats in the garden.

name: they are
title: Present Simple: 'they are'
description: Use 'are' with the plural pronoun 'they' to make simple present statements with the verb 'to be'.
example: They are my friends.

name: they are not
title: Present Simple Negative: 'they are not'
description: Add 'not' after 'are' (or use the contraction 'aren't') to make negative statements with 'they' using the verb 'to be'.
example: They are not at home today.

name: too ADJ/ADV to+INFINITIVE
title: too + Adjective/Adverb + to-infinitive
description: 'Too + adjective/adverb + to-infinitive' shows that something is excessive to the point that a result becomes impossible, e.g. 'too tired to walk'.
example: It's too cold to go swimming today.

name: we are
title: To Be: We are (present simple)
description: Use 'are' with the subject 'we' to describe facts or states about a group that includes the speaker.
example: We are neighbors.

name: we are not
title: To Be: We are not (negative)
description: Add 'not' after 'are' to make a negative statement about 'we', usually contracted to 'we're not' or 'we aren't'.
example: We aren't ready yet.

name: were it not for ...
title: 'Were it not for' (formal inversion)
description: This is the formal, inverted version of 'if it were not for': 'if' is dropped and 'were' moves before the subject to express a present hypothetical dependence on something.
example: Were it not for the rain, we'd be at the beach now.

name: whether
title: Whether (noun clauses and alternatives)
description: 'Whether' introduces a clause expressing a choice between options, used after verbs like know, ask, or decide, often with 'or not'.
example: I'm not sure whether he's coming tonight.
